title: The dative: dem, der, den (Der Dativ)
summary: The third case. After mit, zu, bei, aus, nach, von and seit, der becomes dem and die becomes der. Now am Montag, zum Frühstück and mit Milch finally make sense.
goals: Use the dative after mit, zu, bei, aus, nach, von and seit
Know the dative forms: dem, der, dem, den
Understand the short forms zum, zur, beim, vom, im, am

nicosWeg.title: Nicos Weg A1, chapter 10: Orientation (Wo ist der Bahnhof?, Mit Bus und Bahn)

points: The dative marks the person something is given to or done for: the indirect object. Ask [[Wem?]] (to whom?): [[Die Mutter kauft der Tochter ein Kleid.]]
Definite articles: [[der]] becomes [[dem]], [[die]] becomes [[der]], [[das]] becomes [[dem]], plural [[die]] becomes [[den]], and the plural noun adds -n: [[den Kindern]].
Indefinite: [[einem]] (masculine and neuter), [[einer]] (feminine); no plural. Negative: [[keinem]], [[keiner]], [[keinen]] (plural, noun + -n).
The endings to remember: -em for masculine and neuter, -er for feminine, -en for plural.
Some verbs always take the dative, even with only one object: [[danken]] and [[helfen]]: [[Ich danke dem Mann.]], [[Ich helfe der Frau.]]

notes.extra: The dative as the indirect object ([[Wem?]]), which the lesson leaves for later; it starts with the prepositions.

points: The dative is used in four places. First, the indirect object, usually the person an action is for: [[Die Eltern geben dem Sohn einen Kuli.]] With two objects, the person is usually the dative.
Second, after the dative prepositions: [[aus]], [[bei]], [[mit]], [[nach]], [[seit]], [[von]], [[zu]], [[gegenüber]]: [[Ich fahre mit dem Auto.]]
Third, after dative verbs, which need no accusative: [[Das Buch gehört mir.]], [[Wir können Ihnen helfen.]]
Fourth, with some adjectives, for how you feel: [[Mir ist kalt.]] (I'm cold), [[Mir ist langweilig.]] (I'm bored)
Pronouns change too: [[ihr]] (to her), as in [[Das ist Eva. Ich schenke ihr eine Schokolade.]]

points: After a dative preposition the article changes: [[Er kommt nach dem Unterricht.]], [[Ich esse Nudeln mit einer Gabel.]] The main ones: [[von]], [[zu]], [[aus]], [[ab]], [[seit]], [[nach]], [[mit]], [[bei]], [[gegenüber]].

[[von]]: from a place or person ([[ein Geschenk von meinem Vater]]), from ... to ([[von Montag bis Freitag]]). [[vom]] = [[von dem]]. [[aus]]: out of ([[aus der Flasche]]), a country ([[aus England]]), a material ([[aus Gold]]).
[[mit]]: with ([[Kaffee mit Zucker]]), by a vehicle ([[mit dem Bus]]), at an age ([[Mit achtzehn darf man Auto fahren.]]).

[[nach]]: after ([[nach dem Unterricht]]), to a country or city ([[nach Spanien]]), and in times ([[Viertel nach vier]]). [[zu]]: to a person or place ([[zu meinen Eltern]], [[zum Arzt]], [[zur Schule]]).
[[bei]]: at a company ([[bei BMW]]), near ([[Potsdam liegt bei Berlin.]]), at someone's home ([[bei ihren Eltern]]). [[beim]] = [[bei dem]].

Time: [[seit]] = since or for, up to now ([[seit drei Jahren]]); [[ab]] = from ... on ([[ab Montag]]). [[gegenüber]] = opposite, and it can come after the noun: [[gegenüber dem Bahnhof]], [[mir gegenüber]].

points: Possessives in the dative work like [[einem]] and [[einer]]: -em for masculine and neuter, -er for feminine, -en for plural.
The indirect object receives the direct object: in [[Ich gebe meinem Mann einen Kuss.]], my husband gets the kiss.
All four: [[meinem Mann]], [[meiner Tochter]], [[meinem Baby]], [[meinen Kindern]]. The plural noun adds -n, unless it already ends in -n: [[ihren Nachbarn]].
It works the same for every possessive: [[seinem Bruder]], [[ihrer Schwester]], [[unserem Vater]], [[unseren Großeltern]].
[[euer]] loses an e again: [[eurem]], [[eurer]], [[euren]].

points: [[aus]] means out of the inside of something; [[von]] means from the outside of it, its surface or near it.

Out of the school building: [[Sie kommt aus der Schule.]] From near the school (the school bus): [[Sie kommt von der Schule.]] Out of the fridge: [[aus dem Kühlschrank]]; from on top of it: [[vom Kühlschrank]].
More [[von]]: [[Er kommt gerade von der Arbeit.]], who something is from ([[ein Geschenk von meinem Vater]]), and from ... to ([[von Montag bis Freitag]], [[von Frankfurt bis Paris]]).
More [[aus]]: countries and cities ([[Er kommt aus Vietnam.]]), materials ([[aus Gold]]), and feelings, without an article ([[aus Liebe]], out of love).
Some verbs come with them: [[abhängen von]] (depend on), [[sich erholen von]] (recover from), [[bestehen aus]] (consist of).

sections.title: The third case
sections.text:
You know two cases: the subject ([[der Mann]], the nominative) and the object ([[den Mann]], the accusative, Unit 4). The third is the **dative**. Most often it comes after a few small words: [[mit]], [[zu]], [[bei]], [[aus]], [[nach]], [[von]], [[seit]]. After these, always the dative:
- [[mit dem Bus]] ([[der Bus]])
- [[mit der U-Bahn]] ([[die U-Bahn]])
- [[mit dem Fahrrad]] ([[das Fahrrad]])
- [[mit den Kindern]] ([[die Kinder]])

You've used it since Unit 3 without knowing: [[am Montag]] is [[an dem Montag]], [[zum Frühstück]] is [[zu dem Frühstück]], and [[mit Milch]] is a dative too, just without an article to show it.

sections.title: Two things to notice
sections.text:
- Masculine and neuter are the same: [[dem]], [[einem]], [[meinem]]. Feminine is [[der]], [[einer]], [[meiner]]: yes, the same [[der]] as masculine in the nominative.
- In the plural the noun gets an extra -n: [[die Kinder]], [[mit den Kindern]]. Not when it already ends in -n or -s: [[mit den Eltern]], [[mit den Autos]].

sections.title: The seven dative words
sections.text:
- [[mit]] = with; by: [[mit meiner Freundin]], [[mit dem Bus]]
- [[zu]] = to (a person, a place): [[zu meiner Mutter]], [[zum Arzt]]
- [[bei]] = at someone's place, at a company: [[bei meinen Eltern]], [[bei Siemens]] (Unit 1), [[beim Arzt]]
- [[aus]] = from, out of: [[aus der Schweiz]], [[aus dem Büro]]
- [[nach]] = after; to (cities, countries): [[nach dem Kurs]], [[nach Salzburg]], [[nach Hause]]
- [[von]] = from, of: [[von meinem Bruder]], [[vom Bahnhof]]
- [[seit]] = since, for: [[seit Montag]], [[seit einem Jahr]]

Russian needs three cases where German has one: с мамой (instrumental), к маме (dative), у мамы (genitive). German says [[mit meiner Mutter]], [[zu meiner Mutter]], [[bei meiner Mutter]]: always the dative. And German puts the ending mostly on the article; only the dative plural adds -n to the noun.

sections.title: seit + the present
sections.text: [[Ich wohne seit einem Jahr in München.]] = I **have lived** in Munich for a year. English uses 'have lived'; German, like Russian (Я живу в Мюнхене уже год), uses the present tense, because it's still true.

sections.title: The chunks from Units 3-5, explained
sections.text:
- [[am Montag]], [[am Abend]]: [[an dem]]
- [[am dritten Mai]]: [[an dem]], and [[dritten]] gets -en after [[dem]]
- [[im Mai]], [[im Sommer]]: [[in dem]]
- [[in der Nacht]]: [[die Nacht]] becomes [[der Nacht]] in the dative
- [[am See]] (Unit 5): [[an dem See]], a place: Wo? + dative, lesson 2
- [[Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!]] (Unit 3): [[zu dem]]
- [[zum Frühstück]]: [[zu dem]]
- [[mit Milch]], [[mit Karte]]: dative, but no article to show it
- [[zu Hause]], [[nach Hause]]: fixed phrases with an old dative -e

[[Tut mir leid]], [[Es schmeckt mir]] and [[Können Sie mir helfen?]] come in lesson 5.
